pages.text: A village temple's tier follows the acropolis:$(li)$(l)No acropolis yet$(): open altar, coefficient $(l)1.0$(), 2 worshippers at a time.$(li)$(l)Naiskos$() (Archaic acropolis): $(l)1.5$(), 4.$(li)$(l)Prostyle Temple$(): $(l)2.0$(), 7.$(li)$(l)Peripteral Temple$(): $(l)3.0$(), 10.$(br)The $(l)coefficient$() multiplies favor: the higher the tier, the more each prayer gives.

A temple never upgrades by itself. The village has to $(l)rebuild the acropolis in place$(). Work can start once the village reaches the Classical or Heroic age; materials come from the village store and builders lay it block by block. Promoting here moves the village into the new age too.$(br2)Once the rebuild is finished, the new coefficient applies at once.

Columns, roof tiles, braziers, the cult statue, pediments and the altar are the temple's $(l)key parts$(). For every part missing, the coefficient drops in proportion, but never below 30%%.$(br2)A promotion needs the tier and a $(l)condition$() of at least 80%%. Missing parts become repair requests; if nobody takes them, villagers repair them after a few days.

Greek builders favored two plans: the prostyle, with a row of columns before the door, and the peripteral, with columns all around the cella.$(br2)The Prostyle and Peripteral Temples are built to these plans.
